subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Define professionalism. Explain the characteristics of professionalism and its attributes in nursing – accountability, competence, commitment, integrity and collaboration.

diagram.caption: Attributes of professionalism in nursing
labels: with an outer ring of respect

answer_html:
Introduction A profession is an occupation that requires specialised knowledge and skill acquired through prolonged education, serves society, follows a code of ethics and regulates its own members. Professionalism is the way a member of a profession thinks, behaves and conducts himself or herself while practising that profession.

Definition Professionalism in nursing is the consistent demonstration of the knowledge, skills, values and behaviours expected of a nurse – competent, ethical, accountable and compassionate practice that puts the patient's interest first and upholds the dignity of the profession. It is shown not only in what a nurse knows, but in how she behaves when no one is watching.

Characteristics of professionalism

  1. Specialised knowledge and skill applied with sound clinical judgement.
  2. Service orientation – the welfare of the patient and community comes before personal gain or convenience.
  3. Adherence to a code of ethics and professional standards laid down by regulatory and professional bodies.
  4. Responsibility and autonomy – making decisions within one's scope of practice and taking responsibility for them.
  5. Lifelong learning – updating knowledge through continuing education, reading and research.
  6. Respect for others – patients, families, colleagues and other professionals.
  7. Self-regulation – reflecting on one's own practice and correcting mistakes; supporting the regulation of the profession.
  8. Professional appearance and demeanour, reliability and punctuality.
  9. Effective communication and teamwork.
  10. Contribution to the profession – participation in professional organisations, teaching, research and policy.

Attributes of professionalism 1. Accountability

  • Being answerable for one's actions and omissions – to the patient, the profession (nursing council), the employer, the law and one's own conscience.
  • Examples: documenting care accurately and promptly; reporting one's own errors (e.g. a missed dose) honestly; following up on delegated tasks; practising only within one's scope and competence; explaining the reasons for one's decisions.
  • Accountability is supported by responsibility (the duty to perform a task) and authority (the right to act).

2. Competence

  • Having and using the knowledge, skills, attitudes and judgement needed to provide safe, effective care.
  • Competence develops gradually – Patricia Benner described five stages: novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient and expert.
  • Maintained through continuing nursing education, skill practice, certification courses (BLS, ACLS), self-assessment and recognising one's limits and seeking help.
  • Example: a nurse unfamiliar with a new infusion pump learns its use before connecting it to a patient.

3. Commitment

  • Dedication to patients, the profession and the organisation – doing one's duty fully, even when it is difficult.
  • Examples: punctuality, completing care before handing over, staying calm and caring during heavy workloads, serving during epidemics and disasters (as nurses did during COVID-19), and commitment to quality improvement and learning.

4. Integrity

  • Honesty and consistency between one's values, words and actions; adhering to moral and ethical principles.
  • Examples: never falsifying records or vital signs; admitting mistakes; refusing bribes or improper gifts; not misusing hospital drugs or supplies; maintaining confidentiality; showing moral courage to speak up against unsafe or unethical practices.

5. Collaboration

  • Working together with patients, families and the health team towards shared goals, with mutual respect and open communication.
  • Examples: taking part in multidisciplinary rounds; clear handovers using SBAR; clarifying doubtful orders politely; resolving conflicts constructively; involving patients and families in care decisions; coordinating with community health workers for continuity of care.

Other important attributes – respect for human dignity, caring and compassion, altruism, ethical conduct, cultural competence, advocacy, leadership and professional appearance.

Importance of professionalism

  • Builds public trust and the image of nursing.
  • Ensures patient safety and quality care.
  • Promotes teamwork and a positive work environment.
  • Protects the nurse legally and ethically.
  • Increases job satisfaction and the professional growth of nurses.

Professionalism in daily nursing practice – examples

  • Arriving on time, receiving a complete handover and checking all patients before starting routine work.
  • Introducing oneself by name and role, explaining procedures and asking permission before touching the patient.
  • Following the rights of medication administration and double-checking high-alert drugs, even when the ward is busy.
  • Writing accurate, timely and legible notes, and never signing for care one has not given.
  • Admitting an error promptly, informing the doctor and filing an incident report.
  • Keeping conversations about patients private and avoiding gossip in corridors, lifts and on social media.
  • Treating every patient – rich or poor, conscious or unconscious – with equal respect and attention.
  • Asking for help or supervision when a task is beyond one's competence.
  • Guiding students patiently and setting a good example.

Factors that promote professionalism – sound education and role models, a supportive and ethical work environment, adequate staffing, continuing education, recognition of good practice, and the nurse's own commitment and reflection.

Conclusion Professionalism is the demonstration of a nurse's knowledge, skill, ethics and values in everyday practice. Its key attributes – accountability, competence, commitment, integrity and collaboration – together with respect, caring and lifelong learning, earn the trust of patients and society and give nursing its identity as a profession.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain professional conduct in nursing – following rules and policies, the code of conduct, dress code, professional etiquette and behaviour – and the role of the nurse in maintaining professionalism.
tags: role of nurse in maintaining professionalism
National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act 2023
answer_html:
Introduction Professional conduct is the behaviour expected of a nurse as a member of the nursing profession, as described in laws, regulations, codes of ethics and conduct, and institutional policies. Good conduct protects patients and the reputation of the profession; unprofessional conduct can lead to disciplinary and legal action.

A. Following rules, policies and laws

  • Practise within the legal scope of nursing practice and one's own competence.
  • Maintain valid registration with the State Nursing Council and renew it as required. Nursing is regulated by the Indian Nursing Council and State Nursing Councils; the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023 has been enacted to replace the INC with a National Commission, and until the Commission is constituted the INC continues its regulatory role.
  • Follow hospital policies, protocols and standard operating procedures – medication administration, infection control, biomedical waste rules, consent, medico-legal cases, narcotic drug registers.
  • Report incidents, errors and near-misses through the proper channel.
  • Respect the rights of patients and the laws that protect them.

B. Code of professional conduct The codes of ethics and professional conduct for nurses expect the nurse to:

  • Respect the dignity, rights and uniqueness of every person, without discrimination on grounds of caste, religion, gender, economic status or disease.
  • Maintain privacy and confidentiality.
  • Maintain competence and give evidence-based care.
  • Keep honest, accurate records.
  • Maintain professional relationships and boundaries with patients and families.
  • Work in harmony and collaboration with colleagues and the health team.
  • Avoid conflicts of interest – e.g. not accepting commissions or promoting commercial products for personal gain.
  • Never work while impaired by alcohol or drugs.
  • Report unsafe or unethical practice and act as the patient's advocate.
  • Be a role model for students and juniors and contribute to the advancement of the profession.

C. Dress code

  • Clean, neat, well-fitting uniform as prescribed by the institution, with a visible name badge.
  • Short, clean nails, no nail polish or artificial nails (infection control); hair neatly tied, cap if required.
  • Minimal jewellery – no dangling earrings, bangles or rings with stones that harbour microbes or injure patients.
  • Clean, closed, non-slip footwear; no strong perfume.
  • Uniform not worn outside the hospital, to prevent spread of infection.
  • Purposes – identification, professional image, infection control, safety, and patient confidence.

D. Professional etiquette and behaviour

  • Punctuality and regular attendance.
  • Greet and introduce oneself with name and role; address patients respectfully by name, not by bed number or disease.
  • Polite language and tone, patience, active listening, and respect for patients' privacy (knocking, screening).
  • Respect for seniors, colleagues and other health workers; no gossip or criticism of colleagues in front of patients.
  • Avoid personal phone calls and social media use in patient areas; never post patient information or photographs.
  • Handle complaints calmly and courteously; give proper handover; respect cultural and religious practices.
  • Follow institutional policy on gifts; avoid favouritism.

E. Professional relationships

  • With patients – therapeutic, caring and within boundaries.
  • With colleagues – teamwork, mutual help and constructive feedback.
  • With doctors and other professionals – collaboration, clear communication, clarifying doubtful orders.
  • With students – supervision, teaching and role modelling.

F. Unprofessional conduct (misconduct)

  • Negligence, absence from duty without notice, abuse or neglect of patients, breach of confidentiality, false documentation, theft or diversion of drugs, practising without valid registration, sexual misconduct, and bribery.
  • Consequences – departmental disciplinary action, suspension or removal of the nurse's name from the register by the nursing council, and civil or criminal liability.

G. Role of the nurse in maintaining professionalism

  1. Self-awareness and reflection – regularly reviewing one's own practice and attitudes.
  2. Continuing professional development – attending CNEs, workshops and certification courses; reading journals.
  3. Following the code of ethics and conduct in every situation.
  4. Role modelling and mentoring students and new nurses.
  5. Membership and participation in professional organisations such as TNAI.
  6. Participation in research, audit and quality improvement.
  7. Advocacy for patients and for the profession – speaking up against unsafe practices.
  8. Self-care and work–life balance to prevent burnout.
  9. Positive public image through courteous behaviour, health education in the community and responsible use of media.

Conclusion Professional conduct means practising within the law and policies, following the code of professional conduct, maintaining a proper dress code, behaving with courtesy and respect, and keeping professional relationships. By reflecting, learning continuously, role modelling and advocating, every nurse maintains the professionalism on which public trust in nursing depends.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Differentiate between personal identity and professional identity. Explain how a nurse develops professional identity and preserves self-integrity.
answer_html:
Introduction Every nurse is both an individual and a professional. Personal identity answers the question "Who am I as a person?"; professional identity answers "Who am I as a nurse?". A mature nurse integrates the two without losing her moral integrity.

A. Personal identity versus professional identity

  • Meaning – Personal identity is the individual's sense of self: personality, values, beliefs, culture, family roles and interests. Professional identity is the sense of oneself as a member of the nursing profession – thinking, acting and feeling like a nurse.
  • Source – Personal identity develops from childhood through family, culture, religion and life experience. Professional identity develops through nursing education, clinical experience, role models and professional socialisation.
  • Content – Personal identity includes personal likes, beliefs and lifestyle. Professional identity includes the knowledge, skills, values, ethics and norms of nursing.
  • Expression – Personal identity is expressed in private and social life. Professional identity is expressed in practice – conduct, decisions and relationships with patients and the team.
  • Guided by – Personal identity is guided by personal values. Professional identity is guided by the code of ethics, standards and laws.

B. Development of professional identity

  1. Nursing education – knowledge of the profession's history, values and ethics.
  2. Clinical experience – caring for patients, taking responsibility and seeing the results of care.
  3. Role models and mentors – observing and learning from good teachers and senior nurses.
  4. Professional socialisation – internalising the norms and culture of nursing.
  5. Reflection – reflective journals and discussions about experiences.
  6. Symbols and rituals – lamp-lighting and oath-taking ceremonies, uniform, registration.
  7. Participation in professional organisations, conferences and research.
  8. Feedback and recognition from patients, teachers and colleagues.

C. Preserving self-integrity Self-integrity is the wholeness of the self – acting consistently with one's moral values. It may be threatened when personal values conflict with professional duties (e.g. MTP or end-of-life decisions), when a nurse is pressured to follow unethical orders, or when heavy workloads prevent good care. Ways to preserve self-integrity

  • Value clarification – knowing one's own values and limits.
  • Knowing the code of ethics, patients' rights and the law.
  • Moral courage – speaking up respectfully when something is wrong.
  • Conscientious objection where permitted – informing the supervisor in advance and arranging alternative care, but never refusing emergency or life-saving care or abandoning a patient.
  • Seeking support from mentors, supervisors or the ethics committee.
  • Reflective practice, self-care and healthy boundaries between work and personal life.
  • Honesty in documentation and communication, even when it is difficult.

Conclusion Personal identity reflects who a nurse is as a person; professional identity reflects who she is as a nurse. Professional identity grows through education, experience, role models and socialisation. Self-integrity is preserved by clarifying values, knowing the code and the law, speaking up with courage, seeking support and never compromising the patient's safety.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain professional boundaries in the nurse–patient relationship.

diagram.caption: Continuum of professional behaviour
labels: "zone of helpfulness" (therapeutic relationship) in the centre
over-involvement on the right leading to boundary crossings and boundary violations

answer_html:
Introduction The nurse–patient relationship is a therapeutic relationship that exists for the benefit of the patient. Because the nurse has knowledge, authority and access to the patient's body and personal information, while the patient is ill and dependent, there is an imbalance of power. Professional boundaries are the limits that protect the space between the nurse's power and the patient's vulnerability, keeping the relationship safe and therapeutic.

1. Continuum of professional behaviour

  • Under-involvement – distance, coldness, neglect, disinterest.
  • Zone of helpfulness – the ideal therapeutic relationship: caring, empathetic, focused on the patient's needs.
  • Over-involvement – the nurse's personal needs enter the relationship, leading to boundary crossings and violations.

2. Boundary crossing

  • A brief, sometimes harmless departure from usual professional behaviour, often for the patient's benefit, after which the nurse returns to the professional role – e.g. a comforting hug for a grieving relative, sharing a small personal fact to build rapport, accepting a token gift such as sweets on a festival as per policy.
  • Repeated crossings can lead to violations, so they need awareness and reflection.

3. Boundary violation

  • An action that exploits the relationship to meet the nurse's personal needs and harms the patient – e.g. romantic or sexual relationships with patients (sexual misconduct is always a violation), borrowing money or accepting expensive gifts, financial exploitation, keeping secrets with a patient, excessive personal self-disclosure, abusive or demeaning behaviour, and using information about the patient for personal gain.

4. Warning signs (red flags)

  • Spending excessive time with one patient; visiting the patient off duty.
  • Giving personal phone numbers or connecting on social media.
  • Feeling that "only I understand this patient"; becoming defensive when colleagues comment.
  • Keeping secrets or selectively reporting the patient's behaviour.
  • Flirting, discussing one's personal problems, giving or receiving gifts or money.
  • Changing schedules to be with the patient.

5. Maintaining professional boundaries

  • Keep the focus on the patient's needs; use therapeutic communication.
  • Limit self-disclosure to what helps the patient.
  • Follow institutional policies on gifts, social media and contact after discharge.
  • Use a chaperone during intimate examinations and procedures.
  • Be careful of dual relationships (e.g. caring for neighbours or relatives in small communities) and maintain confidentiality.
  • Consult a supervisor when unsure; reflect on one's feelings; transfer care if objectivity is lost.
  • Document interactions clearly.

6. Special settings – psychiatric units, paediatric and home-care settings, and long-term care need extra vigilance because patients are more vulnerable.

Conclusion Professional boundaries protect the therapeutic nurse–patient relationship from exploitation. Nurses should recognise the difference between occasional boundary crossings and harmful boundary violations, watch for warning signs, and maintain boundaries through patient-focused communication, limited self-disclosure, policies, supervision and reflection.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain professional socialisation in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Professional socialisation is the process by which a person acquires the knowledge, skills, values, attitudes, norms and identity of a profession – the process of "becoming a nurse". It begins when a student enters nursing school and continues throughout the career, as the nurse moves from student to staff nurse, specialist, teacher or manager.

1. Outcomes of professional socialisation

  • Internalisation of the values and ethics of nursing.
  • Development of professional identity and role confidence.
  • Competence in the knowledge and skills of the role.
  • Commitment to the profession.

2. Models of professional socialisation A. Davis's model of doctrinal conversion (six stages)

  1. Initial innocence – the student enters with a lay image of nursing (helping, caring for the sick) and feels uncomfortable when reality differs.
  2. Labelled incongruity – the student recognises and shares with peers the gap between expectations and the real nursing role.
  3. Psyching out – the student identifies what teachers expect and begins to behave accordingly.
  4. Role simulation – the student performs the expected behaviours, at first feeling "acted".
  5. Provisional internalisation – the student begins to believe in and identify with the professional role, though doubts remain.
  6. Stable internalisation – the professional values and behaviours become part of the student's own identity.

B. Benner's model of skill acquisition – novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient and expert, showing growth from rule-based to intuitive, experience-based practice.

C. Reality shock (Kramer) – new graduates often experience a gap between school ideals and workplace realities, passing through honeymoon, shock, recovery and resolution phases; support during this period prevents burnout and dropout.

3. Factors influencing professional socialisation

  • Educational environment – curriculum, teaching methods and clinical exposure.
  • Faculty and clinical role models – their attitudes and behaviour.
  • Peers and student groups.
  • Preceptors and mentors during internship and early employment.
  • Organisational culture – workload, teamwork, recognition, ethical climate.
  • Personal factors – motivation, values, self-concept.
  • Family and society – the image of nursing, gender expectations, media.

4. Role of educators and organisations

  • Positive role modelling by teachers and senior nurses.
  • Orientation and preceptorship programmes for new nurses.
  • Mentoring, reflective journals, debriefing and case discussions.
  • Involvement of students in professional activities – Student Nurses' Association, conferences, community service.
  • Ceremonies such as lamp-lighting and oath-taking.
  • Supportive work environments, feedback and recognition.

Conclusion Professional socialisation transforms a student into a nurse by gradually internalising the profession's knowledge, values and identity. Models such as Davis's six stages and Benner's novice-to-expert stages describe this journey. Good role models, mentoring, preceptorship and supportive environments help nurses through reality shock and towards a stable professional identity.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain the challenges of professionalism in nursing in India and the strategies to overcome them.
tags: National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act 2023
answer_html:
Introduction Nursing in India has grown into a recognised profession with degree, postgraduate and doctoral programmes, but many factors still make it difficult for nurses to practise with full professionalism.

A. Challenges

  1. Shortage of nurses and heavy workload – high nurse–patient ratios, long shifts and extra non-nursing duties reduce the time for quality care and lead to burnout.
  2. Poor working conditions and low salaries, especially in some private institutions, with job insecurity and contractual employment.
  3. Image and gender stereotypes – nursing is sometimes seen as a subordinate or "women's job" rather than a knowledge-based profession.
  4. Limited autonomy and hierarchical relationships – nurses may not be included in decision-making.
  5. Variable quality of education – rapid growth of institutions with inadequate faculty and clinical facilities.
  6. Limited career ladder and advanced practice roles – few positions for nurse practitioners and specialists.
  7. Migration of trained nurses abroad for better pay and conditions.
  8. Workplace violence and harassment against health workers.
  9. Lack of continuing education and time for professional development.
  10. Unqualified persons performing nursing duties in some settings.
  11. Ethical pressures – commercialisation of health care, conflicts of interest, misuse of social media.
  12. Regulatory transition – the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023 has been enacted to modernise regulation, but the new Commission is yet to be fully established.

B. Strategies to overcome them

  1. Adequate staffing according to norms, fair salaries, safe working hours and job security.
  2. Safe workplaces – protection against violence and harassment, security measures and supportive policies.
  3. Quality education – accreditation, qualified faculty, good clinical exposure and competency-based curricula (such as the INC 2021 B.Sc curriculum).
  4. Continuing professional development – regular CNEs, in-service education, e-learning and certification courses; linking re-registration to continuing education.
  5. Career pathways and advanced practice – nurse practitioner, specialist and leadership positions.
  6. Leadership development and representation of nurses in policy-making bodies.
  7. Strong professional organisations (TNAI and specialty associations) to advocate for nurses.
  8. Mentoring and preceptorship for new nurses.
  9. Research and evidence-based practice to strengthen the knowledge base and visibility of nursing.
  10. Positive public image through media, community health education and recognition of nurses' contributions (e.g. the National Florence Nightingale Award).
  11. Well-being programmes to prevent burnout and support mental health.
  12. Personal commitment of each nurse to ethics, competence and courteous conduct.

Conclusion Professionalism in Indian nursing is challenged by shortages, workload, working conditions, image, limited autonomy, variable education, migration and violence. Adequate staffing, safe workplaces, quality education, continuing development, career pathways, leadership, strong organisations and individual commitment can help nurses practise with the professionalism the public deserves.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Differentiate between accountability and responsibility.
answer_html:
Responsibility

  • The duty or obligation to carry out a task or role that has been assigned or accepted – it is about "what I must do".
  • It can be shared or delegated (e.g. a nurse may delegate bed-making to an attendant).

  • Example: the nurse is responsible for giving the 8 a.m. medicines to her patients. Accountability

  • Being answerable for the outcome of one's actions and decisions – to the patient, profession, employer, law and self – it is about "I must explain and justify what I did".

  • It cannot be delegated – the nurse who delegates a task remains accountable for the decision to delegate and for supervision.
  • Example: if a dose is missed, the nurse reports it, explains what happened and takes corrective action. Responsibility is the duty; accountability is answerability for how the duty was carried out.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: What is a boundary violation? Give two examples.
answer_html:
A boundary violation is an act in which a nurse crosses the limits of the professional relationship to meet her own personal, emotional, sexual or financial needs, so that the relationship becomes exploitative and harmful to the patient. Unlike a brief boundary crossing, a violation always damages trust and is unprofessional conduct. Examples

  1. Entering into a romantic or sexual relationship with a patient (sexual misconduct is always a violation).
  2. Borrowing money, accepting expensive gifts or involving a patient in personal business. Other examples – keeping secrets with a patient, excessive personal self-disclosure, and contacting the patient on social media for personal relationships.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: State the purposes of a dress code for nurses.
answer_html:
A dress code is the set of rules about uniform and appearance laid down by an institution. Its purposes are:

  1. Identification – patients and visitors can recognise the nurse, her role and her name (name badge).
  2. Professional image – a neat, clean appearance inspires confidence and trust.
  3. Infection control – short nails, no nail polish or artificial nails, minimal jewellery, tied hair and clean uniforms reduce transmission of microbes; uniforms are not worn outside the hospital.
  4. Safety – closed, non-slip footwear and no dangling jewellery prevent injuries to nurse and patient.
  5. Comfort and freedom of movement for efficient work.
  6. Discipline and uniformity within the nursing team.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Differentiate between a profession and an occupation.
answer_html:
Profession

  • Requires a long period of specialised education with a strong theoretical body of knowledge.
  • Primary motive is service to society; members are guided by a code of ethics.
  • Has autonomy and self-regulation through a statutory council or commission (licensing, registration).
  • Members are accountable for their judgement; there is a lifelong career commitment and a professional organisation.

  • Examples – nursing, medicine, law. Occupation

  • Requires shorter training, often skill-based, learned on the job.

  • Primary motive is earning a living; no binding code of ethics.
  • Regulated mainly by the employer; little autonomy.
  • Examples – driver, clerk, shopkeeper.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Define values. Explain the characteristics and types of values and the process of value formation and value clarification.

diagram.caption: Process of value clarification (Raths, Harmin and Simon)
labels: after considering consequences; Prizing – cherishing the choice
affirming it publicly; Acting – acting on the choice

answer_html:
Introduction Every decision a nurse makes – how she speaks to a patient, whether she reports an error, how she responds to a request for information – is influenced by her values. Understanding one's own values, and those of patients, is the foundation of ethical and culturally sensitive care.

Definition Values are enduring beliefs or ideals about what is good, right, desirable or important, which guide a person's choices, attitudes and behaviour. Rokeach described a value as an enduring belief that a particular mode of conduct or end-state of existence is personally or socially preferable. A person's values arranged in order of importance form a value system.

Characteristics of values

  1. Learned – acquired from family, culture, religion, education and experience; not inborn.
  2. Relatively enduring – stable over time, but can change with new experiences and reflection.
  3. Hierarchical – some values are more important than others for a person.
  4. Guide behaviour and decisions – they act as standards for judging actions.
  5. Emotional component – people feel strongly about their values and defend them.
  6. Influence attitudes and beliefs.
  7. Vary between individuals, families, cultures and generations.
  8. May conflict with each other or with the values of others.
  9. Often unconscious until they are examined (clarified).

Types of values A. According to Rokeach

  • Terminal values – desirable end-states: health, happiness, freedom, peace, wisdom, salvation.

  • Instrumental values – preferred ways of behaving to reach those ends: honesty, courage, responsibility, kindness, self-discipline. B. According to the source or area of life

  • Personal values – an individual's own beliefs (e.g. family loyalty, hard work).

  • Professional values – those of the profession (human dignity, integrity, altruism, autonomy, social justice).
  • Cultural and societal values – shared by a community (respect for elders, hospitality).
  • Moral or ethical values – about right and wrong (truthfulness, non-violence).
  • Religious and spiritual values – derived from faith.
  • Organisational values – of an institution (quality, patient safety).
  • Others – aesthetic, economic, political and intellectual values. C. Intrinsic and extrinsic values – valued for their own sake (e.g. health) or as a means to something else (e.g. money).

Value formation Values are formed gradually through:

  1. Modelling – children imitate parents, teachers and admired persons.
  2. Moralising – being taught what is right and wrong by family, religion and school.
  3. Laissez-faire – exploring and developing values freely with little guidance.
  4. Rewarding and punishing – behaviours that are rewarded are reinforced.
  5. Responsible choice – being allowed to make choices and experience their consequences. - Agents – family, school, peers, religion, media, culture, and later professional education and the work environment. - Stages – in childhood values are accepted from parents; in adolescence they are questioned and influenced by peers; in adulthood a stable value system develops, though it continues to evolve. Moral development (Kohlberg) moves from obeying rules for fear of punishment, to following social rules, to acting on universal ethical principles.

Value clarification Value clarification is the process by which a person becomes aware of his or her own values, their sources and their relative importance, so that choices become conscious and consistent. Raths, Harmin and Simon described seven steps in three phases:

  1. Choosing
    • (1) choosing freely, without pressure;
    • (2) choosing from alternatives;
    • (3) choosing after thoughtful consideration of the consequences of each alternative.
  2. Prizing
    • (4) cherishing the choice and being happy with it;
    • (5) affirming the choice publicly when appropriate.
  3. Acting
    • (6) acting on the choice;
    • (7) repeating the action consistently, so that it becomes a pattern of life. A belief that meets all seven criteria is a true value.

Methods of value clarification – value-ranking exercises, values grids, value sheets with reflective questions, journal writing, case discussions and role play.

Importance for nurses

  • Self-awareness – nurses avoid imposing their own values on patients (e.g. about diet, family planning, lifestyle).
  • Helping patients clarify their values – for decisions such as surgery, end-of-life care or family planning.
  • Resolving value conflicts with patients, families and colleagues.
  • Ethical decision-making – clear values support consistent and justifiable decisions.
  • Professional growth – aligning personal and professional values.

Nurse's role in helping clients clarify values – listen without judging; ask open-ended questions ("What matters most to you?"); help the client list alternatives and consequences; reflect feelings; support the client's own decision.

Conclusion Values are learned, enduring beliefs that guide behaviour; they may be terminal or instrumental, personal, professional, cultural, moral or religious. They are formed through modelling, moralising, rewards and responsible choices, and are clarified through the seven steps of choosing, prizing and acting. Value clarification helps nurses understand themselves, respect patients' values and make sound ethical decisions.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain the core professional values of nursing – human dignity, integrity, altruism, autonomy and social justice – with examples from practice.

diagram.caption: Core professional values of nursing
labels: social justice – around a centre labelled "patient-centred nursing"
with an outer ring of caring

answer_html:
Introduction Professional values are the standards of action and attitude accepted by the nursing profession that guide nurses' behaviour and decisions. The American Association of Colleges of Nursing identified five core values – human dignity, integrity, altruism, autonomy and social justice. Caring, confidentiality and accountability are also essential values. They are learned through education and socialisation and are reflected in the codes of ethics.

1. Human dignity Meaning – respect for the inherent worth and uniqueness of every person, regardless of age, caste, religion, gender, economic status, illness or behaviour. In practice

  • Addressing patients by name and introducing oneself.
  • Protecting privacy during examination, bathing and elimination (screens, covering).
  • Respecting cultural and religious practices.
  • Treating unconscious, confused and dying patients with the same respect as others; caring for the dead body with dignity.
  • Caring for patients with stigmatised conditions (HIV, leprosy, mental illness, drug use) without discrimination.

2. Integrity Meaning – acting in accordance with an appropriate code of ethics and accepted standards of practice; honesty, truthfulness and consistency between words and actions. In practice

  • Recording only what was actually observed and done; never "pre-charting" or falsifying vital signs.
  • Reporting one's own errors and near-misses.
  • Giving honest information within one's role; not making false promises.
  • Refusing to take part in fraud, unnecessary procedures or misuse of drugs and supplies.

3. Altruism Meaning – concern for the welfare and well-being of others, putting the patient's needs before one's own convenience. In practice

  • Staying to help a colleague during an emergency even after the shift ends.
  • Spending time to comfort an anxious or dying patient.
  • Volunteering during disasters, epidemics and health camps; donating blood.
  • Mentoring students and junior nurses.

4. Autonomy Meaning – respecting the right of patients to make decisions about their own health care, based on adequate information and free from pressure. In practice

  • Giving information needed for informed consent and checking understanding.
  • Respecting a patient's informed refusal of treatment while explaining the consequences.
  • Involving patients in planning their care (e.g. choosing the time of bath or diet options).
  • Respecting advance directives.
  • Professional autonomy – the nurse also exercises independent judgement within her scope of practice.

5. Social justice Meaning – upholding moral, legal and humanistic principles of fairness; ensuring equal treatment and fair access to health care for all. In practice

  • Providing care based on need, not on status, influence or ability to pay.
  • Helping poor patients access free services and schemes such as Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY.
  • Advocating for vulnerable groups – women, children, the elderly, tribal and migrant populations, persons with disabilities.
  • Supporting fair allocation of scarce resources and speaking against discrimination.

6. Other essential values

  • Caring – compassion, presence and attention to the whole person.
  • Confidentiality – protecting the patient's personal and health information.
  • Accountability – taking responsibility for one's actions and their outcomes.
  • Respect, trust, competence and teamwork.

Importance of professional values

  • Guide ethical decision-making in difficult situations.
  • Build trust between nurses, patients and society.
  • Give nursing its professional identity and improve the quality and safety of care.
  • Provide standards for evaluating nursing conduct.

Professional values in action – common situations

  1. A poor patient cannot afford the prescribed medicines (social justice) – the nurse informs him about free medicines and diagnostics in government hospitals, Jan Aushadhi stores and Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY coverage, and involves the medical social worker.
  2. Staff avoid a patient with HIV (human dignity) – the nurse gives the same quality of care using standard precautions, protects his confidentiality and gently corrects colleagues' misconceptions.
  3. The nurse realises she missed a dose of antibiotic (integrity) – she informs the doctor, gives the dose as advised, documents honestly and files an incident report rather than hiding the mistake.
  4. A diabetic patient refuses insulin (autonomy) – the nurse explores his fears (needles, cost, myths), educates him and his family, involves the doctor, and respects his final informed decision while continuing to support him.
  5. An elderly patient is frightened at night (altruism and caring) – although the ward is busy, the nurse spends a few minutes reassuring her, leaves a light on and checks on her regularly.
  6. A relative asks for details of another patient's illness (confidentiality) – the nurse politely declines and shares information only with those entitled.

Threats to professional values – heavy workloads and staff shortages, commercial pressures, hierarchy and fear of speaking up, burnout and indifference. Nurses protect their values through reflection, teamwork, supportive leadership and adherence to the codes of ethics.

Conclusion The core professional values of nursing – human dignity, integrity, altruism, autonomy and social justice – along with caring, confidentiality and accountability, are expressed in everyday actions: protecting privacy, honest records, putting patients first, respecting their choices and ensuring fair care for all. Living these values makes nursing a trusted profession.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Differentiate between personal and professional values. Explain value conflicts in nursing and how they can be resolved.
answer_html:
Introduction A nurse brings her personal values into the profession and acquires professional values through education and practice. Usually they agree, but when they differ – or when the nurse's values differ from those of patients, colleagues or the organisation – value conflicts arise.

A. Personal versus professional values

  • Source – Personal values come from family, culture, religion and life experiences. Professional values come from nursing education, codes of ethics and professional socialisation.
  • Scope – Personal values guide an individual's private life. Professional values guide conduct in nursing practice.
  • Uniformity – Personal values vary widely from person to person. Professional values are shared by all members of the profession.
  • Written form – Personal values are usually unwritten. Professional values are written in codes of ethics and standards.
  • Accountability – Personal values are judged by one's conscience and community. Professional values are enforced by employers and regulatory councils.

B. Types of value conflict in nursing

  1. Intrapersonal – conflict within the nurse, e.g. a nurse who personally opposes abortion is assigned to care for a woman undergoing legal MTP.
  2. Nurse and patient – e.g. a patient refuses blood transfusion on religious grounds, or refuses surgery that the nurse believes is necessary.
  3. Nurse and family – e.g. the family wants aggressive treatment or wants to hide the diagnosis from the patient, while the patient wishes to know.
  4. Nurse and colleagues or doctors – e.g. disagreement about pain relief, a DNR decision or an unsafe order.
  5. Nurse and organisation – e.g. cost-cutting, short staffing or pressure to discharge early, which conflicts with quality care.
  6. Cultural conflicts – differences in beliefs about illness, gender roles or decision-making.

C. Resolving value conflicts

  1. Value clarification – the nurse identifies her own values and recognises the other person's values.
  2. Focus on the patient's rights and best interests; respect the informed choices of competent patients.
  3. Use the code of ethics, institutional policy and law as guides.
  4. Open, respectful communication – listen, explain, negotiate and seek common ground.
  5. Ethical decision-making model – define the problem, gather facts, consider options and consequences, decide and evaluate.
  6. Consultation with the supervisor, senior colleagues or the ethics committee.
  7. Conscientious objection where allowed – inform the supervisor early so that another nurse provides care; never abandon a patient or refuse emergency care.
  8. Documentation of discussions and decisions.
  9. Self-reflection and support to cope with moral distress.

Conclusion Personal values guide private life, while professional values are shared, written standards for practice. Conflicts may arise within the nurse or with patients, families, colleagues or the organisation. They are resolved by clarifying values, focusing on the patient's rights, following the code and law, communicating openly, consulting others and, where necessary, conscientious objection without abandoning the patient.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Define advocacy. Explain the role of the nurse as a patient advocate and the barriers to advocacy.
answer_html:
Definition Advocacy means speaking or acting on behalf of another person to protect his or her rights, interests and well-being. Patient advocacy in nursing is the active support of the patient's rights and choices – informing, supporting, protecting and, when necessary, speaking up for the patient.

1. Models of advocacy

  • Rights-protection model – the nurse is the guardian of the patient's rights (to information, consent, privacy, safe care) and reports violations.
  • Values-based decision model – the nurse helps the patient discuss needs and options and make decisions consistent with his own values, without imposing her own.
  • Respect-for-persons model – the nurse acts to protect the dignity, privacy and choices of the patient; when the patient cannot decide (unconscious, child, severely ill), the nurse acts in his best interests.

2. Role of the nurse as a patient advocate

  1. Informing – ensuring the patient has understandable information about the illness, treatment, alternatives and costs.
  2. Supporting decisions – respecting the patient's informed choices, even when the nurse would choose differently.
  3. Ensuring valid consent – checking that the patient has understood before signing.
  4. Protecting from harm – questioning unclear or unsafe orders, reporting errors, negligence or abuse, preventing falls and infections.
  5. Protecting privacy, dignity and confidentiality.
  6. Speaking for vulnerable patients – unconscious, mentally ill, children, elderly, disabled, poor and illiterate patients.
  7. Mediating between the patient, family and health team; arranging interpreters.
  8. Ensuring access to care and entitlements – government schemes, free medicines and diagnostics, referral services.
  9. Community and policy advocacy – campaigning for safe water, sanitation, immunisation, tobacco control and better health policies.

3. Barriers to advocacy

  • Hierarchy and power imbalance – fear of conflict with doctors or administrators.
  • Fear of retaliation or losing one's job; lack of legal protection.
  • Lack of knowledge, confidence or assertiveness skills.
  • Heavy workload and lack of time.
  • Lack of institutional support and unclear policies.
  • Conflict of loyalty between the patient and the employer.
  • Cultural factors – family-centred decision-making, patients who do not wish to question authority.
  • Uncertainty about what is in the patient's best interest.

4. Overcoming barriers – education in ethics, law and assertive communication; supportive policies and ethics committees; teamwork; documentation; professional organisations that support nurses; and moral courage.

Conclusion Advocacy is acting on behalf of patients to protect their rights and well-being. Through informing, supporting decisions, protecting from harm and speaking for the vulnerable, the nurse serves as the patient's advocate, overcoming barriers such as hierarchy, fear, lack of knowledge and workload with education, institutional support and courage.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain the ICN Code of Ethics for Nurses (2021) – its fundamental responsibilities and four elements.
answer_html:
Introduction The International Council of Nurses (ICN), a federation of national nurses' associations (including TNAI from India), first adopted an international Code of Ethics for Nurses in 1953. It has been revised several times; the latest revision was in 2021. It is a guide for action based on social values and needs, used by nurses throughout the world.

1. Fundamental responsibilities of nurses Nurses have four fundamental responsibilities: to promote health, to prevent illness, to restore health and to alleviate suffering (including promoting a dignified death). The need for nursing is universal, and nursing care is respectful of human rights – including cultural rights, the right to life and choice, dignity and being treated with respect – without discrimination on grounds such as age, colour, culture, ethnicity, disability or illness, gender, sexual orientation, nationality, politics, language, race, religious or spiritual beliefs, legal, economic or social status.

2. The four elements of the Code Element 1 – Nurses and patients or other people requiring care

  • The nurse's primary professional responsibility is to people requiring nursing care.
  • Promotes an environment in which human rights, values, customs and spiritual beliefs are respected.
  • Ensures people receive accurate, understandable information for consent; maintains confidentiality and privacy.
  • Promotes equity and social justice in access to care; shows professional values such as respect, compassion, trustworthiness and integrity.

Element 2 – Nurses and practice

  • The nurse carries personal responsibility and accountability for ethical practice and for maintaining competence through continuous learning.
  • Maintains fitness to practise and personal standards of conduct that reflect well on the profession.
  • Uses technology and scientific advances in ways compatible with the safety, dignity and rights of people.
  • Promotes a culture of safety and takes appropriate action when care is endangered by colleagues, systems or others.

Element 3 – Nurses and the profession

  • Nurses take a leading role in determining and implementing standards of clinical practice, management, research and education.
  • Contribute to evidence-informed practice and research.
  • Participate in professional organisations and help create positive practice environments with safe and fair working conditions.
  • Support and respect colleagues; challenge unethical behaviour.

Element 4 – Nurses and global health

  • Nurses value health care as a human right and support universal access.
  • Work towards global goals such as the Sustainable Development Goals, and respond to emergencies, disasters, conflicts and epidemics.
  • Address the social determinants of health and protect the natural environment from harmful effects (climate change, pollution).
  • Collaborate with other professions and the public to promote health.

3. Uses of the Code

  • Guide for ethical practice and decision-making.
  • Basis for nursing education and national codes (such as the INC code of ethics).
  • Standard for regulation, management and research.
  • Tool for self-reflection and peer review; it helps the public understand what to expect from nurses.

Conclusion The ICN Code of Ethics (2021) sets out nurses' four fundamental responsibilities and four elements – nurses and patients, nurses and practice, nurses and the profession, and nurses and global health. It guides nurses everywhere to give respectful, competent, safe and equitable care and to contribute to the profession and to global health.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain the importance of professional values in transcultural nursing care.
tags: professional values in culturally diverse care
answer_html:
Introduction Transcultural nursing (developed by Madeleine Leininger) is the area of nursing that studies and compares cultures in order to provide culturally congruent care – care that fits the beliefs, values and practices of the patient. India's great diversity of religions, languages, regions, food habits, family patterns and health beliefs makes this especially important. Professional values guide the nurse to respect this diversity.

1. Professional values applied to transcultural care

  • Human dignity – every culture is respected; customs are not ridiculed; patients are not labelled by caste, religion or region.
  • Social justice and non-discrimination – equal quality of care for all; attention to disadvantaged and tribal groups.
  • Autonomy – respecting how a patient wishes decisions to be made. In many Indian families, decisions are taken jointly; the nurse respects this while ensuring the patient's own wishes are heard.
  • Caring – showing compassion in ways meaningful to the patient (e.g. allowing family members to stay, respecting rituals).
  • Confidentiality – clarifying with the patient what may be shared with which family members.
  • Integrity and veracity – honest, understandable information, using interpreters where needed.
  • Altruism – going beyond routine to meet cultural needs (e.g. arranging a vegetarian or Jain diet, prayer time).

2. Cultural aspects nurses must consider

  • Communication – language, gestures, eye contact, touch and modesty; preference for same-gender caregivers.
  • Food habits – vegetarianism, fasting days, halal food, food taboos during illness or after childbirth.
  • Religious practices – prayers, sacred threads, kara, rosaries, holy water; rituals at birth and death.
  • Health beliefs – hot and cold foods, evil eye, karma, use of Ayurveda, home remedies and faith healers.
  • Family structure – joint families, the role of elders and mothers-in-law in decisions.

3. Approaches to culturally competent care

  • Leininger's three modes of nursing action:
    • Culture care preservation or maintenance – supporting beneficial practices (e.g. breastfeeding, family support).
    • Culture care accommodation or negotiation – adapting care to harmless practices (e.g. allowing a sacred thread during surgery when safe).
    • Culture care repatterning or restructuring – helping change harmful practices (e.g. applying cow dung to the umbilical cord, delaying colostrum).
  • Campinha-Bacote's model of cultural competence – cultural awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters and desire.
  • Cultural humility – lifelong self-reflection and learning from patients.
  • Avoid ethnocentrism (believing one's own culture is superior) and stereotyping.

4. Importance

  • Builds trust and improves communication and cooperation.
  • Improves adherence to treatment and health outcomes.
  • Reduces conflicts, discrimination and health inequities.
  • Respects human rights and the dignity of every patient.

Conclusion Professional values – human dignity, social justice, autonomy, caring, confidentiality, integrity and altruism – are the basis of transcultural nursing. By understanding cultural beliefs and using preservation, accommodation and repatterning, nurses give culturally congruent, respectful and effective care to India's diverse population.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain the strategies for developing and strengthening professional values in nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Professional values are not acquired automatically with a degree; they must be consciously developed, practised and reinforced throughout a nurse's education and career. Strategies operate at the level of the individual, the educational institution, the organisation and the profession.

A. Individual level

  1. Self-reflection and value clarification – examining one's own values and how they influence practice.
  2. Studying the codes of ethics (INC, ICN) and patients' rights.
  3. Reflective journals and learning from experiences, including mistakes.
  4. Learning from role models and seeking mentors.
  5. Lifelong learning – CNEs, ethics workshops and reading.
  6. Participation in professional organisations, community service and research.
  7. Self-care – a rested, healthy nurse is better able to act on her values.

B. Educational level

  1. Integration of values and ethics into the curriculum – the INC 2021 course on professionalism, values and ethics in the fourth semester.
  2. Active teaching methods – case studies of ethical dilemmas, ethics rounds, role play, simulation, debates, storytelling and value-clarification exercises.
  3. Faculty role modelling – teachers who show respect, honesty and fairness.
  4. Clinical supervision and mentoring – discussing value-related experiences in the ward.
  5. Rituals and symbols – lamp-lighting and oath-taking ceremonies, uniforms, pledges.
  6. Student Nurses' Association activities, community outreach and service learning.
  7. Evaluation of the affective domain – assessing attitudes and behaviour, not only knowledge.

C. Organisational level

  1. Ethical climate – clear policies, open communication and zero tolerance for abuse and dishonesty.
  2. Supportive leadership that encourages questions and reporting of errors without fear (just culture).
  3. Adequate staffing and resources, so that nurses are not forced to compromise care.
  4. Recognition and rewards – appreciation, awards (such as the National Florence Nightingale Award), career advancement.
  5. Ethics committees, ethics consultation and debriefing after difficult cases.
  6. Orientation, preceptorship and in-service education on values and ethics.
  7. Peer support and staff well-being programmes.

D. Professional and societal level

  • Standards and codes of the regulatory bodies and TNAI; positive media image of nurses; public awareness of nurses' roles; nurses' participation in policy-making.

Conclusion Professional values are developed and strengthened through individual reflection and learning, values-based education with good role models and active teaching methods, supportive organisational cultures with recognition and ethics resources, and strong professional standards. Together these help nurses live their values consistently in practice.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain caring as a core value of nursing and the caring behaviours of a nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Caring is often described as the essence of nursing. Leininger called caring the central and unifying focus of nursing, and Jean Watson described nursing as a human caring science, built on a transpersonal caring relationship between nurse and patient. Caring means genuine concern for the well-being of another person, expressed through attention, compassion and skilful action.

1. Swanson's theory of caring – five caring processes

  1. Knowing – striving to understand the patient's experience as it is for him, avoiding assumptions.
  2. Being with – being emotionally present, sharing feelings without burdening the patient.
  3. Doing for – doing for the patient what he would do for himself if he could – comforting, protecting, anticipating needs, preserving dignity.
  4. Enabling – helping the patient through transitions and unfamiliar events by informing, explaining, supporting and validating feelings.
  5. Maintaining belief – sustaining faith in the patient's capacity to get through an event and face the future with meaning and hope.

2. Caring behaviours of a nurse

  • Presence – being attentive and available, sitting at the bedside, making eye contact.
  • Attentive listening – letting the patient tell his story; responding to feelings.
  • Comforting touch – holding a hand, gentle positioning (with respect for cultural norms).
  • Providing physical comfort – relief of pain, hygiene, positioning, warmth, rest.
  • Explaining and informing – reducing fear through clear information.
  • Involving patients and families in decisions and care.
  • Respecting individuality – preferences, culture, religion and privacy.
  • Timely response to calls and needs; competence and skill in procedures (skilled care is also caring).
  • Honesty, patience and kindness, especially with anxious, angry or confused patients.
  • Spiritual care – supporting prayer, faith and the search for meaning.
  • Family care – supporting relatives, especially in critical illness and at the end of life.

3. Importance of caring

  • Promotes healing, comfort and a sense of safety.
  • Builds trust and improves communication and cooperation.
  • Increases patient satisfaction and adherence to treatment.
  • Gives meaning and satisfaction to the nurse's work.

4. Barriers to caring – heavy workload and shortage of staff, task-oriented routines, focus on technology, burnout and compassion fatigue, poor working conditions. Promoting caring – adequate staffing, self-care and support for nurses, role modelling, reflective practice and recognition of caring behaviour.

Conclusion Caring is the heart of nursing, expressed through knowing, being with, doing for, enabling and maintaining belief. Presence, listening, comforting, informing, respecting individuality and skilful care are caring behaviours that heal, build trust and give meaning to nursing, and organisations must support nurses so that they can continue to care.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: What is value clarification?
answer_html:
Value clarification is the process by which a person becomes aware of his own values, their sources and their priorities, so that his choices and actions become conscious and consistent.

  • According to Raths, Harmin and Simon, it has three phases and seven steps:
    • Choosing – freely, from alternatives, after considering the consequences;
    • Prizing – cherishing the choice and affirming it publicly;
    • Acting – acting on the choice and repeating it as a consistent pattern.
  • Importance for nurses – increases self-awareness, prevents imposing personal values on patients, helps patients make value-based decisions, and supports ethical decision-making.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Define altruism. Give two examples from nursing practice.
answer_html:
Altruism is a core professional value meaning unselfish concern for the welfare and well-being of others, in which the nurse places the patient's needs before her own convenience or gain. Examples

  1. Staying beyond duty hours to help a colleague manage an emergency admission or a cardiac arrest.
  2. Spending extra time comforting an anxious patient before surgery, or sitting with a dying patient who has no family. Other examples – volunteering in disaster relief and health camps, donating blood, and mentoring students without expecting rewards.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: What is human dignity? How does a nurse preserve it?
answer_html:
Human dignity is the inherent worth and uniqueness of every person, which must be respected regardless of age, caste, religion, gender, economic status, illness or behaviour. It is a core professional value of nursing. Ways a nurse preserves human dignity

  • Addressing patients by name and introducing oneself; speaking politely.
  • Protecting privacy – screens, covering the body, knocking before entering.
  • Respecting choices, culture and religious practices.
  • Caring for unconscious, confused, dying and stigmatised patients with the same respect.
  • Maintaining confidentiality and caring for the dead body respectfully.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Define ethics and morality. Explain the major ethical theories with examples from nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses face moral questions every day – whether to tell the truth to a dying patient, how to divide limited time among many patients, or whether to follow an order that seems unsafe. Ethics gives a reasoned basis for such decisions.

Definitions

  • Ethics (Greek ethos – character, custom) is the branch of philosophy that systematically studies what is right and wrong, good and bad, in human conduct, and the reasons that justify actions. Nursing ethics applies these principles to the practice of nursing.
  • Morality (Latin mores – customs) refers to the personal and social standards of right and wrong behaviour that people learn from family, culture and religion and follow in daily life.

Ethics and morality compared

  • Morality is personal or cultural, often accepted without questioning; ethics is a formal, reasoned study of those standards.
  • Morality answers "What do I believe is right?"; ethics asks "Why is it right, and how should we decide?"
  • Professional ethics are written in codes (INC, ICN) and are shared by all members of the profession.
  • Law sets the minimum standards enforced by the State; ethics often asks for more than the law (e.g. kindness, truthfulness), and some legal acts may still be ethically debated.

Branches – meta-ethics (meaning of moral terms), normative ethics (theories of what is right) and applied ethics (bioethics, nursing ethics, business ethics).

Major ethical theories 1. Deontology (duty-based ethics) – Immanuel Kant

  • An action is right or wrong in itself, according to duties and rules, regardless of its consequences.
  • Kant's categorical imperative – act only on principles that you would want everyone to follow; and treat every person as an end in himself, never merely as a means.
  • Duties include telling the truth, keeping promises and respecting persons.
  • Nursing example – a nurse keeps a patient's confidence and does not lie to him, even when a lie would make the moment easier.
  • Limitation – rigid; gives little help when two duties conflict.

2. Teleology (consequence-based ethics) – Utilitarianism (Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill)

  • An action is right if it produces the greatest good (happiness, health) for the greatest number of people.
  • Act utilitarianism judges each act; rule utilitarianism follows rules that generally produce the best results.
  • Nursing examples – mass immunisation programmes, triage during disasters, allocating ICU beds to those most likely to benefit.
  • Limitation – may ignore the rights of individuals or minorities; consequences are hard to predict.

3. Virtue ethics – Aristotle

  • Focuses on the character of the person rather than on rules or results – what would a good, virtuous nurse do?
  • Virtues include compassion, honesty, courage, justice, patience and practical wisdom, developed through practice.
  • Nursing example – a nurse shows compassion and courage by staying calm and truthful with a frightened family during an emergency.
  • Limitation – does not give clear guidance in specific dilemmas.

4. Ethics of care – Carol Gilligan, Nel Noddings

  • Emphasises relationships, responsibility, compassion and attention to the context and vulnerability of the person, rather than abstract rules.
  • It is very close to the nature of nursing.
  • Nursing example – a nurse considers the patient's family situation, fears and cultural background when planning discharge, not only the medical facts.
  • Limitation – may be seen as subjective or partial.

5. Principlism – Beauchamp and Childress

  • Uses four principles – autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice – to analyse and balance ethical problems in health care; widely used in clinical ethics.
  • Nursing example – before an operation, the nurse ensures informed consent (autonomy), the expected benefit (beneficence), safety measures (non-maleficence) and fair scheduling (justice).
  • Limitation – principles may conflict and must be weighed.

6. Rights-based ethics

  • Every person has rights (to life, liberty, privacy, information, health care) that others are obliged to respect.
  • Nursing example – upholding the Charter of Patients' Rights – right to information, second opinion, privacy and non-discrimination.
  • Limitation – rights can conflict, and rights need corresponding responsibilities.

7. Other approaches

  • Casuistry – reasoning from similar earlier cases (paradigm cases).
  • Natural law theory (Thomas Aquinas) – actions that agree with human nature and reason are right; it gave rise to the principle of double effect.

Use of ethical theories in nursing

  • No single theory solves all problems; nurses combine them to understand, justify and explain their decisions, guided by codes of ethics, law and patients' values.

Conclusion Ethics is the reasoned study of right and wrong conduct, while morality is the set of personal and cultural standards people live by. Deontology, utilitarianism, virtue ethics, ethics of care, principlism and rights-based ethics each offer a different lens – duty, consequences, character, relationships, principles and rights – and together they help nurses make sound and defensible ethical decisions.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: Explain the ethical principles – autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, veracity, fidelity and confidentiality – with their application in nursing and the conflicts between them.
answer_html:
Introduction Ethical principles are basic, widely accepted guides that help nurses decide what is right in a given situation. The four principles of Beauchamp and Childress – autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice – are supplemented in nursing by veracity, fidelity and confidentiality.

1. Autonomy (self-determination)

  • Meaning – respecting the right of a person with decision-making capacity to make informed, voluntary decisions about his own body and care.
  • Conditions – the patient must have capacity, receive adequate information in understandable language, and decide without pressure.
  • Application – informed consent before procedures; respecting informed refusal (e.g. a patient refuses amputation); respecting advance directives; involving patients in care planning; offering choices (time of bath, diet).
  • Limits – children, unconscious patients and those with severe mental illness may lack capacity (a guardian or nominated representative decides in their best interests); autonomy may be limited when it seriously harms others (e.g. isolation in infectious TB).
  • In Indian families decisions are often taken jointly; the nurse respects this while making sure the patient's own wishes are heard.

2. Beneficence (doing good)

  • Meaning – the duty to act for the benefit of the patient, promote well-being and prevent and remove harm.
  • Application – pain relief, comfort measures, health teaching, early mobilisation, timely response to calls, helping patients access schemes and services.
  • Caution – doing "what is best" without respecting the patient's wishes becomes paternalism.

3. Non-maleficence (doing no harm)

  • Meaning – "first, do no harm" (primum non nocere) – avoiding intentional harm and minimising the risk of harm.
  • Application – checking the rights of medication administration, preventing falls, infections and pressure injuries, maintaining competence, refusing to carry out unsafe orders, avoiding neglect and abuse.
  • Principle of double effect – an action with a good intention (e.g. morphine to relieve pain at the end of life) is acceptable even if it carries a foreseen but unintended harmful effect (e.g. respiratory depression), provided the harm is not the means to the good and the benefit outweighs the risk.

4. Justice (fairness)

  • Meaning – treating people fairly and equally, and distributing benefits, burdens and resources fairly (distributive justice).
  • Application – care according to need, not status or ability to pay; triage in emergencies; fair allocation of nursing time according to patient acuity; non-discrimination (HIV, caste, religion, gender); helping poor patients obtain free services.
  • Criteria – equal shares, need, merit, maximum benefit – each has strengths and weaknesses.

5. Veracity (truthfulness)

  • Meaning – the duty to tell the truth and not deceive.
  • Application – honest, understandable information about illness and care; truthful documentation; no false reassurance ("everything will be fine") when it is not true; supporting the doctor in breaking bad news.
  • Therapeutic privilege – rarely, information may be delayed if it would cause serious harm, but it should never become a reason for routine concealment.

6. Fidelity (faithfulness)

  • Meaning – keeping promises and commitments and being loyal to the patient.
  • Application – returning at the promised time with pain medicine; following through on care; maintaining trust; not abandoning patients.
  • Conflict – loyalty to the patient versus loyalty to the employer or colleagues.

7. Confidentiality

  • Meaning – protecting personal and health information shared in the professional relationship, disclosing it only to those entitled.
  • Application – discussing patients only with the care team; protecting records and electronic data; privacy in wards.
  • Exceptions – patient's consent, continuity of care, notifiable diseases, medico-legal cases, court orders, and serious risk to others. For example, under the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017, a doctor or counsellor may inform a partner at significant risk, after counselling the patient and informing him of the intention to disclose.

Accountability – being answerable for one's actions – runs through all the principles.

Conflicts between principles – examples

  1. Autonomy vs beneficence – a competent patient refuses life-saving surgery; the nurse explains the consequences, explores reasons and respects the informed refusal.
  2. Veracity vs non-maleficence – the family asks the nurse not to tell a patient that he has cancer; the nurse explores the family's fears and the patient's wish to know, and involves the doctor in gradual, supportive disclosure.
  3. Justice vs beneficence – one ventilator and two patients needing it; transparent triage criteria are used.
  4. Confidentiality vs protecting others – an HIV-positive patient refuses to inform the spouse; counselling and the legal procedure for partner notification are followed.
  5. Autonomy vs non-maleficence – an elderly patient insists on walking alone despite a high fall risk; the nurse negotiates supervised walking and a safer environment.

Resolving conflicts – weigh the principles in the specific situation, consider the patient's values, follow the code and law, use an ethical decision-making model, consult colleagues or the ethics committee, and document decisions.

Conclusion Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, veracity, fidelity and confidentiality guide every aspect of nursing – from consent and safe medication to fair allocation of care and truthful communication. When principles conflict, nurses must weigh them thoughtfully, respecting the patient's values and the law, to reach the most ethical decision.

subject: Professionalism, Professional Values and Ethics including Bioethics
question: What is an ethical dilemma? Explain the common ethical dilemmas in nursing and describe an ethical decision-making model, with an example.

diagram.caption: Steps of ethical decision-making
labels: identify the ethical problem and principles involved
identify the people involved and their values
choose and justify the best option

answer_html:
Definition An ethical dilemma is a situation in which a nurse must choose between two or more alternatives, each supported by ethical principles, so that choosing one means not fulfilling another – there is no clearly right answer, and any choice has some undesirable consequence.

  • It differs from moral uncertainty (being unsure which principles apply) and moral distress (knowing what is right but being prevented by constraints from doing it).

Common ethical dilemmas in nursing

  1. Truth-telling and collusion – relatives ask that a patient should not be told his diagnosis of cancer.
  2. Refusal of treatment – a patient refuses blood transfusion or surgery, or wants to leave against medical advice because of cost.
  3. End-of-life decisions – DNR orders, withdrawal of ventilator support, a patient asking to end his life.
  4. Allocation of scarce resources – one ICU bed or ventilator and several patients; limited nursing staff.
  5. Confidentiality versus protecting others – an HIV-positive or TB patient who will not inform family members.
  6. Informed consent in illiterate, elderly, confused or frightened patients, or when relatives sign without the patient's understanding.
  7. Use of restraints in confused or agitated patients – safety versus freedom and dignity.
  8. Following orders that seem harmful – e.g. a drug dose that appears wrong.
  9. Reporting a colleague's error, impairment or abuse (whistle-blowing) versus loyalty.
  10. Beginning-of-life issues – requests for sex determination, MTP, care of extremely premature babies.
  11. Mandatory reporting – a pregnant adolescent who asks that her case not be reported under the POCSO Act.
  12. Special treatment for VIPs while other patients wait; acceptance of gifts.

Ethical decision-making models A. General steps (similar to the nursing process)

  1. Gather the facts – medical situation, prognosis, patient's capacity, wishes, family situation, legal requirements, policies.
  2. Identify the ethical problem and the principles in conflict.
  3. Identify the people involved (patient, family, nurse, doctor, institution) and their values and roles; decide who has the authority to decide.
  4. List the possible options and the likely consequences of each.
  5. Choose the best option and be able to justify it using ethical principles, the code of ethics and law.
  6. Act on the decision.
  7. Evaluate the outcome and reflect on what was learnt. B. The MORAL model – Massage the dilemma (identify issues and the views of all parties), Outline the options, Review criteria and Resolve, Affirm the position and Act, Look back and evaluate. C. Thompson and Thompson's bioethical decision model – a ten-step model: review the situation; gather additional information; identify the ethical issues; identify personal and professional moral positions; identify the moral positions of key individuals; identify value conflicts; determine who should make the decision; identify the range of actions and outcomes; decide and carry out the action; evaluate the results. D. The four-box (four topics) method (Jonsen, Siegler and Winslade) – examines medical indications (beneficence and non-maleficence), patient preferences (autonomy), quality of life, and contextual features (family, cost, law, religion, justice).

Example – applying the steps Situation – Mr. R, 68 years, has advanced lung cancer. His sons ask the nurse not to tell him the diagnosis. That evening Mr. R asks the nurse, "Am I going to die? Nobody tells me anything."

  1. Facts – Mr. R is alert and has decision-making capacity; the disease is incurable; he wants information; the sons fear he will lose hope.
  2. Ethical problem – veracity and autonomy (his right to know and plan) versus the family's wish to protect him (beneficence and non-maleficence as they see it).
